b: While I’ve always aspired to read the Dune series, I never seem to find the time before the next Dune movie comes out. The books are long, and the new movies directed by Denis Villeneuve are so good. I have found success reading the Dune series through comics though.

Frank Herbert’s son, Brian Herbert, along with Kevin J. Anderson, have adapted the iconic series into graphic novel format. These books have given me a satisfying taste of the story paired with beautiful art of the desolate yet mesmerizing world of Dune.

The series includes three volumes, Dune: The Graphic Novel Book 1, Book 2: Muad’Dib, and Book 3: The Prophet. The gorgeous illustrations by Raúl Allén and Patricia Martín immerse you right into the landscape of the bleak and breathtaking desert planet. The character art is compelling and helps show their feelings and motivations, rather than just tell them through narrative.

The new Dune film, Dune: Part Three, releases in theaters December 18th. While the Dune graphic novels offer a great way to catch up on the series before you see the movie, I also have comics for Dune fans who want to fall into similar stories.

Each comic below touches upon various themes that make Dune special. Between their pages, you’ll travel across wasteland planets crawling with curious creatures, immerse in political intrigue amongst warring nobility, and follow space wanderers on desperate quests.
Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind by Hayao Miyazaki

Hayao Miyazaki’s manga series is a must-read for Dune fans. Like Paul Atreides, Nausicaä steps into a prophesied savior role in her story, though Nausicaä strives for peace over war. Her world shares many similarities with Dune, with its barren landscapes and powerful Ohmu creatures reminiscent of Dune’s sandworms. As various kingdoms wage war on each other in an effort to control ancient, destructive technology, Nausicaä sets out to try and negotiate peace.

Alexandre Dumas’s The Count of Monte Cristo is a classic tale of corruption, oppression, and revenge, and these themes strongly align with the story of Dune. Ibrahim Moustafa does an incredible job of adapting Dumas’s classic into a sci-fi graphic novel. After getting framed for treason and locked away in a hover-prison, Redxan Samud makes his great escape, puts his new fortune to use, and seeks revenge on those who ruined his life.
Monstress, Volume 1: Awakening by Marjorie M. Liu, Illustrated by Sana Takeda

This epic graphic novel by Marjorie M. Liu includes stunning illustrations by Sana Takeda. The story takes place in an alternate matriarchal 1900’s Asia. Like Paul Atreides, teen Maika possesses powerful psychic abilities. As Maika tries to survive in a dark, war-stricken world, she navigates a curious connection to a monster that will put them both in danger.
On a Sunbeam by Tillie Walden

While this sweet graphic novel by Tillie Walden offers a more quietly-paced sci-fi story than Dune, it does include the theme of searching for someone across space. Just as the Bene Gesserit seek the Kwisatz Haderach in Dune, the protagonist in this book, Mia, looks for her long-lost love. Fans of the epic cinematography of the Dune movies and the vivid descriptions of sci-fi landscapes in the Dune books will also appreciate the breathtaking art of this moving graphic novel.

Like Dune, I hope these comics offer you windows into awe-inspiring and compelling sci-fi worlds. For more good reads for Dune fans, check out these 14 Fascinating Books Like DUNE, or these Best Science Fiction Books of the Century (So Far).
